Each track ends in a **channel strip** in the **mixer**: a fader for its level, a pan control for where it sits left to right,
**mute** and **solo**, and a **meter**. All the strips add up in the **master** strip, which is what you hear and what is saved
when you bounce. The mixer is the same in every DAW; only the colours change.

## The controls

- **Fader**, in **decibels (dB)**. 0 dB leaves the track as it is; −6 dB is about half its voltage, and to the ear a little under half as loud
  takes about −10 dB. Faders move in dB because the ear hears in ratios.
- **Pan**: C is the middle, L100 / R100 hard left / right. Kick, snare, bass and the lead stay in the middle; spread the rest.
- **Mute (M)** silences a track; **Solo (S)** silences every *other* track. Solo is for finding a problem; judge balance with everything playing.
- **Meter**: how loud the track is, with a white **peak** mark. Green is fine, yellow is getting loud, red is close to **0 dBFS**,
  the most a digital file can hold. Past it the waveform is cut off: **clipping**, a harsh crackle. The CLIP light stays lit
  once it happens (click it to reset).

## Fix a bad mix

This mix is wrong on purpose: the keys and guitar are too loud, the bass is nearly gone, the drums are buried, and everything is
in the middle.

1. Play it. Is the master's CLIP light coming on? Pull the **Master** down until it stops, then leave it there.
2. Start with the drums and bass: bring them up until the groove is solid.
3. Bring the keys and guitar **down** until they sit around the groove, not on top of it. Turning things down is most of mixing.
4. Pan the guitar to L40 and the keys to R40. Listen to how they stop fighting.
5. Solo the bass to hear what it's doing, then un-solo. Mute the guitar: is the song better without it?
6. Double-click any fader or pan to put it back to 0 / centre.

<div class="mdaw" data-id="daw-mixer" data-preset="badmix" data-show="transport tracks mixer automation"></div>

### Volume automation (preview)

A fader that moves by itself is **volume automation**. In this DAW, click a track, then **Volume lane** (or press **V**): a lane opens under the
tracks. Click it to add a point and drag the point up or down; double-click a point to remove it. Or use the keyboard: put the playhead where you
want a change, press **A** (a point appears at the level the track already has), then **↑ ↓** change it a decibel and **← →** slide it a beat
(Shift: 6 dB or a bar; Alt: finer), **[ ]** pick the previous or next point, **Delete** removes it, **Esc** leaves. Once a track has points they *are* its level and its fader
locks, marked **(A)**; delete the points to use the fader again. Keys work the vim way too: **h j k l** are the arrows, and a **number first** repeats the next key, so **3k** raises the point 3 dB and **12j** lowers it 12.
Try bringing the keys down under the guitar for the first bars.

### Velocity or volume automation?

Both make a sound louder or quieter, at different places in the chain, so they **multiply** (add, in decibels).

| | Velocity | Volume automation |
|---|---|---|
| Belongs to | One **note** | A whole **track** |
| Set when | The note starts (it cannot change afterwards) | Continuously, any time the track sounds |
| Changes the tone? | Often yes: a soft piano note is also darker (this DAW's piano and electric pianos filter softer notes darker) | No: it only turns the whole sound up or down |
| Can fade a held note? | No | Yes |
| In the MIDI file | The note-on velocity, 1–127 | A separate stream of controller 7 (volume) events |
| Good for | Accents, phrasing, ghost notes, a crescendo you play note by note | Sections (verse quieter than chorus), fades, ducking, rides |

How much does velocity do here? This DAW's instruments follow roughly level = velocity^1.6. That is, velocity 127 is the full level (0 dB), 96 is about
−4 dB, 64 about −10 dB, 32 about −19 dB. (Other programs and instruments use other curves; I have not checked theirs.) So a move of
one velocity step is small and a halving is large.

Two habits keep them from fighting:

1. **Shape the part with velocity first, then balance the track with the fader or automation.** If you turn a track down with automation and then raise every velocity
   to make it audible again, you have thrown away its dynamics.
2. **Use automation for anything that happens *while* a note rings**: a pad that swells, a held organ chord that fades. Velocity cannot do that.

A keyboard-driven way to set velocity is proposed below ("A keyboard flow for velocity"); it is not built yet.

The points are written into the exported MIDI file as controller 7 (volume), and read back from it. Whether your DAW turns those events into
automation, and on which lane, depends on the program: open the file and look. I have not verified what Live and Logic do with them.

### A keyboard flow for velocity (note mode, in progress)

**Part of this is built.** Click a clip in the DAW above and press **Enter**: that is **note mode** (**Esc** leaves). Built so far: the motions, the text objects, the operators **>** **<** **gU** **gu**, **r1**–**r8**, counts, **.** (repeat) and **u** (undo).
Still to come, and marked below: velocity patterns in registers (**y**/**p**), **gq**, **Ctrl-a**/**Ctrl-x**, Visual mode, macros and the **:** command line. The plan is in `apps/shared/daw/TODO.md`.
The idea is to borrow vim's *grammar*: **[count] operator motion**, with the cursor on a note.

**Motions** move the note cursor (they also work after an operator):

| Key | Moves to |
|---|---|
| **h** **l** | previous / next note in time |
| **j** **k** | the note below / above in the same chord |
| **w** **b** **e** | next / previous / last note of the chord ("word") |
| **(** **)** | previous / next beat |
| **{** **}** | previous / next bar |
| **0** **$** | first / last note of the clip |

**Text objects** (after an operator, or in Visual): **iw** the note, **ic** its chord, **ih** its beat, **ib** its bar, **ip** the whole clip, **iv** the top line (the highest note of each chord: the melody).
A count extends them: **2ib** is two bars.

**Operators** (each takes a motion or a text object; doubling the key means "this chord", as **dd** means "this line"):

| Operator | Does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **>** / **<** | louder / quieter by a step (counts multiply it) | **3>ib**: the bar, three steps louder |
| **gU** / **gu** | accent / ghost (vim's upper-case / lower-case) | **gUic**: accent this chord |
| **gq** (to come) | tidy: straighten the velocities into a ramp from the first to the last note | **gq2ib** after setting the ends: a crescendo over two bars |
| **y** / **p** (to come) | yank / put a **velocity pattern** | **"ayib** saves a bar's accent pattern in register *a*; **3"ap** lays it down three times |
| **r** + 1–8 | set to a dynamic: 1 ppp, 2 pp, 3 p, 4 mp, 5 mf, 6 f, 7 ff, 8 fff | **r5** on a chord; **v** then **r4** on a selection |

**Visual mode** (to come): **v** selects notes (**h l** extend), **V** whole chords, **Ctrl-v** a block of time × pitch (on the drum grid: the hi-hat row across four bars). Every operator works on the selection.
**Ctrl-a** / **Ctrl-x** add / take 1 from the velocity, as in vim (the count multiplies); in Visual, **g Ctrl-a** adds 1, 2, 3 … down the selection, which is a ready-made crescendo.

**Repeat and record**: **.** repeats the last change and **u** undoes (built); **qa** … **q** records a key sequence into register *a* and **@a** replays it (so "accent beat 1 of every bar" is one recording and **8@a**).

**Command line** (to come): **:** takes vim-style ranges: **:%vel mf** (everything), **:'<,'>vel 40-100** (a ramp over the selection), **:vel 64** (this chord).

A worked example: you have played a pad with flat velocities. **{** to the first bar, **gUic** accents beat 1; **y** the bar as a pattern (**"ayib**), then **}** and **3"ap** to give the next three bars the same shape;
**Vjj** … then **g Ctrl-a** to swell the last four. Nothing there needs the mouse.

These keys live in the editor's own mode, because in the Arrangement **q** is Quantize, **r** is Record, **v** is the volume lane and **p** places a Session clip. **Enter** with a clip selected opens note mode, so "back to the start" is now **Home**.

The rest of mixing (EQ, compression, reverb on sends, references) is in [Recording 7: Mixing](rec-mixing.qmd); level and headroom before
the mix in [Recording 1: Gain Staging](rec-gain-staging.qmd).

## In other DAWs

<div class="daw-map">

| | BandLab | Ableton Live | Logic Pro |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open the mixer | Mixer button (bottom), or each track's header controls | Session View (**Tab**), or the Mixer section in Arrangement (Cmd/Ctrl+Option/Alt+M) | **X** |
| Fader / pan | Volume and pan on every track header and in the mixer | Track Volume and Pan in the mixer section | Fader and pan knob on each channel strip |
| Mute / solo | M / S on the track | Track Activator (the number button) / S | M / S |
| Master | Master track volume | Main track (Master), far right | Stereo Out strip |
| Effects on a track | Effects (FX) slot on the track | Drag a device onto the track | Audio FX slots on the channel strip |

</div>
